label: Chapter 7 · Part B
title: Common Objections II: Scientism, Other Gods, Evil & Hiddenness
tagline: Why “science says no,” “one god further,” and even suffering do not overturn the proofs
oneSentence: The most popular modern objections to natural theology — scientism, brute-fact laws, the “complex designer,” “one god further,” the gap between the philosophers’ God and the believer’s, evil, hiddenness, suspect motives, and persistent disagreement — either refute themselves, attack a caricature of classical theism, or hold the proofs to a standard nobody applies elsewhere, so none of them touches the five demonstrations.
bigPicture:
This module covers the second half of Feser’s final chapter, where he turns from technical objections to the cosmological argument (Part A) to the broad, culturally dominant reasons people give for dismissing natural theology without examining it. The centerpiece is a long critique of **scientism** — the view that science is the only genuine source of knowledge. Feser treats it at length because it is the unspoken premise behind most New Atheist objections: if only science counts as knowledge, then metaphysical demonstrations can be waved away as unscientific before anyone reads them.

Against scientism Feser presses four problems: it is self-refuting or else trivial; the method of physics cannot in principle give a complete description even of physical reality; the laws of nature that science appeals to cannot be the ultimate explanation of anything; and the main argument for scientism — the predictive and technological success of science — simply does not support it. He then works through eight further objections: that the fundamental laws are a brute fact; that a designer would be more complex than the universe; that theists should go “one god further” and reject their God as they reject Zeus; that the philosophers’ God is not the God of ordinary believers; the problem of evil (both Mackie’s logical version and Rowe’s evidential version); divine hiddenness; the charge that theistic arguments are mere rationalizations; and the claim that no one can have a proof when so many people remain unconvinced.

What unifies the section is a diagnostic pattern worth mastering. Nearly every objection does one of three things: it saws off the branch it sits on (scientism, Hume’s Fork); it attacks a picture of God as one more complex being or hypothesis inside the universe rather than the purely actual, simple, necessary source of all being that the five proofs actually conclude to (the complex designer, one god further, brute-fact laws); or it evaluates strict demonstrations by the wrong standards — probability, parsimony, universal assent, the motives of the arguer. Once you can spot which move is being made, you can answer most popular objections briefly and calmly.

The section is also where the book faces the hardest emotional objection — suffering. Feser offers a **defense** rather than a full **theodicy**: he argues that evil is logically compatible with God and that, given independent proof that God exists and is good, we have reason to think a greater good is drawn from evil even when we cannot see it. For someone who wants to persuade, this is the most delicate ground in the whole course, and this module pays special attention to answering it humanely rather than glibly. The chapter — and the book — ends with Feser’s account of what “demonstration” means and his conclusion that the five proofs stand.
objectives: State the four problems Feser raises against scientism and explain why the first one makes scientism either self-refuting or vacuous.
Use the airplane-engineer and metal-detector analogies to show why the success of physics does not show that physics describes all of reality.

Explain why no account of the “laws of nature” (Aristotelian, Cartesian-Newtonian, Humean, Platonic) lets laws serve as the ultimate explanation of the world, and why treating them as a brute fact fails.
Explain why Hume’s and Dawkins’ “complex designer” objection misses arguments that conclude to an absolutely simple first cause.
Diagnose the “one god further” objection as a category mistake, using the triangularity or Form-of-the-Good analogy.
Distinguish a defense from a theodicy and the logical from the evidential problem of evil, and reconstruct Feser’s replies to Mackie and to Rowe.
Identify the two assumptions behind the divine hiddenness argument and give Feser’s reasons for rejecting each.
Explain what classical theists mean by a “demonstration,” and why controversy or suspect motives do not show that a demonstration fails.
Give a crisp, calm one-line answer to each objection, and respond to someone in real pain over suffering without being glib.

summary.heading: Scientism: the hidden premise and its four problems
summary.body:
Feser defines **scientism** as the view that science alone gives us genuine knowledge, so that the only philosophy worth taking seriously is whatever is already implicit in science. He calls it a key ingredient of the New Atheism and says that, despite the confidence of its defenders, there are no good arguments for it and decisive arguments against it. That is why he spends so long on it: if scientism were true, natural theology could be dismissed unheard.

He lays out four problems in advance:

1. Scientism is self-defeating, and it can escape that only by becoming trivial.
2. Scientific method cannot even in principle give a complete description of reality.
3. The laws of nature through which science explains things cannot in principle give a complete explanation of reality.
4. The main argument for scientism — the predictive and technological success of modern science — has no force.

summary.heading: Problem 1: self-refuting or trivial
summary.body:
The first horn of the dilemma: the claim that science’s methods are the only reliable route to knowledge (Feser cites Alex Rosenberg’s formulation) is not itself a scientific result. No experiment establishes it. In fact, not even the claim that science is *a* rational form of inquiry can be established scientifically, because science rests on philosophical presuppositions: that there is an objective world outside scientists’ minds; that this world has regularities that laws could capture; that our intellects and senses can discover and describe those regularities. Science presupposes these, so it cannot justify them without arguing in a circle. To justify them you must step outside science — and the existence of such an extrascientific standpoint refutes the thesis that only science gives rational access to reality.

Philosophy has also always been needed to *interpret* science: whether the world is made of substances or events, what a cause is, what the universals named in laws (electron, quark) are, and whether theories describe reality at all or are just tools for prediction. Science can shed light on these questions but cannot settle them. Since science depends on philosophy both to justify its starting points and to interpret its results, scientism is doubly false; Feser endorses John Kekes’ verdict that philosophy is a better candidate than science for the model of rationality.

The second horn: the defender of scientism may dig in and say philosophy must therefore be part of science. But then “science” has been redefined to include anything that could be offered against scientism, and the thesis becomes empty. Worse, it becomes consistent with views it was meant to exclude. Aristotle and Aquinas regarded natural theology itself as a science — not mathematical or experimental like physics, but *more* certain than physics, because it rests on strict demonstrations from premises any physical science must assume. If “science” is stretched that far, there is no non-arbitrary way to exclude natural theology. The whole point of invoking scientism was to dismiss natural theology without engaging it; stretched, scientism can no longer do that, and the critic must face the arguments head-on instead of plugging his ears.

summary.heading: Problem 2: science cannot give a complete description of reality
summary.body:
Paradoxically, the very method that makes physics so successful guarantees its incompleteness. Physics describes the world in purely quantitative terms — following Galileo’s image of nature as a book written in mathematics. So of course it discovers the aspects of reality that can be predicted and controlled: those are the only aspects it allows itself to attend to. Everything else slips through its methodological net.

Ordinary experience is qualitative through and through: colors, sounds, tastes, smells, warmth, pains, thoughts, choices, purposes, meanings. Physics abstracts from all that. There is nothing wrong with abstraction as long as we remember we are doing it. Feser’s illustration: engineers working out how many passengers of average weight a plane can carry ignore everything about people except weight — and even ignore actual weights in favor of an average no real person may have. Very useful. But it would be absurd for the people planning in-flight meals and movies to rely only on the engineers’ data, and more absurd to insist that because the data say nothing about food or film preferences, there are no such preferences. The data are silent *because* the method guaranteed they would be.

Physics is no less abstract. If some familiar feature of the world doesn’t appear in physics, that is not a discovery that it isn’t there; the method stipulated in advance that it be left out. Feser recalls Bertrand Russell — no friend of natural theology — who stressed that physics gives only the abstract, mathematical structure of events and says nothing of the intrinsic character of whatever has that structure. And that means physics itself implies there is more to reality than it describes, because there cannot be a structure without something that has the structure.

summary.heading: Problem 3: laws of nature cannot be the ultimate explanation
summary.body:
Science explains by appeal to laws, but any appeal to laws (or to Krauss’ proposed layers of laws) raises the questions of what a law is, how it has any power to do anything, and where it comes from — questions scientific explanation, which presupposes laws, cannot answer. Feser surveys the main philosophical theories of laws and argues that none helps scientism:

- **Aristotelian:** a law is shorthand for how a thing will behave given its nature or essence. Then laws presuppose the existence and activity of the things that follow them, so they cannot explain the existence of those things — and cannot explain the existence of the universe, contra Krauss.
- **Cartesian-Newtonian:** laws are a theological notion — God has set things up to behave in regular ways. Then God does the real explaining, which is no help to an atheist wielding scientism.
- **Humean:** laws merely summarize regularities we happen to observe. Then they tell us *that* a regularity exists, not *why* — they re-describe rather than explain.
- **Platonic:** laws are abstract objects in which physical things “participate.” Then we still need to know why there is a physical world participating in them, and in these laws rather than others — which requires something beyond the laws.

So these are questions only philosophy can answer, because they concern what every scientific explanation takes for granted. Nor can the scientism defender reply that ultimate explanation is unavailable anyway: that is itself a philosophical claim, and a false one, since it violates the principle of sufficient reason defended in chapter 5.

summary.heading: Problem 4: the argument from success is a non sequitur
summary.body:
Why do smart people accept scientism anyway? Borrowing a phrase from Wittgenstein, Feser says a picture holds them captive: the dazzling predictive and technological success of science. Rosenberg argues that the success of physics shows its methods are the right ones for acquiring *all* knowledge and that physics is the whole truth about reality. Many scientism advocates would widen this to include chemistry and biology, but they share the core inference, which Feser reduces to two steps: science’s predictive power and technology are unmatched by any rival source of knowledge; therefore what science reveals is probably all that is real.

That is as bad as arguing that because metal detectors find coins and metal objects better than any other method, metallic objects are probably all that exist. Metal detectors are tuned to one aspect of the world; even a perfect success rate would not make it likely that nothing else exists. Physics brilliantly captures the aspects of nature that can be modeled mathematically — it doesn’t follow that there are no other aspects.

Rosenberg adds that critics of scientism are inconsistent: they trust their cardiologist, mechanic, and software engineer, but cry “scientism” when their music, morals, or metaphysics are subjected to science. Feser replies that this is like saying you can’t trust metal detectors to detect anything unless you think they alone detect physical objects. To object that metal detectors cover part of reality while science covers the whole of it simply begs the question at issue.

The same fallacy appears whenever a scientism advocate demands a list of the predictive successes of metaphysics or theology and declares victory when none is offered — like demanding the metal-detecting achievements of gardening, cooking, and painting and concluding that spades, spatulas, and brushes should be replaced by metal detectors. A method that is very useful for the predictable and controllable aspects of the world does not show those aspects are all there is. Such thinkers resemble the drunk who searches only under the streetlamp because that is where the light is, and concludes the keys can be nowhere else.

summary.heading: Scientism’s fallback positions: “worth knowing” and “conceptual analysis”
summary.body:
A retreat: perhaps science can’t answer every question, but philosophy’s questions lack crisp, consensus answers and produce no technology, so science tells us everything *worth* knowing. Feser gives two replies. First, this is like taking only the classes you know you will ace and then citing your GPA as proof of your brilliance. If only the predictable, controllable, consensus-generating counts as “science,” science will trivially be one long success story — that says nothing about whether the questions it excludes matter. Second, the claim that only such questions are worth pursuing is itself a philosophical claim needing philosophical defense; once again, trying to avoid going beyond science requires going beyond it.

A more sophisticated move (Feser cites James Ladyman and Don Ross’s program of “naturalized” metaphysics): unless philosophy is just an extension of science, all it can be is **conceptual analysis**, which appeals to intuitions and folk notions that may not track reality — it tells us how we think, not how the world is. Feser calls this a false alternative, a variant of **Hume’s Fork** (all objects of inquiry are either relations of ideas or matters of fact). Hume’s Fork is notoriously self-refuting: it is neither a conceptual truth nor an empirically testable fact. The modern version — every legitimate inquiry is either conceptual analysis or natural science — likewise is neither, and no evidence from natural science could support it. (In a footnote he adds that appealing to neuroscience or cognitive science here would beg the question, since whether those sciences are our only source of knowledge about cognition is exactly what is disputed.) The scientism advocate takes up a third cognitive stance toward reality in the very act of denying that one exists.

Moreover, the truths of **logic and mathematics** fit neither tine: they have a necessity natural science lacks and an objectivity mere conceptual analysis cannot guarantee. Attempts to deny their necessity or objectivity face notorious difficulties (see chapter 3), and the only motive for them is to save scientism. The truths of natural theology, Feser argues, are like these: necessary and objective yet neither empirical-scientific nor merely conceptual. If the scientism advocate cannot see how such knowledge is possible, that is his problem: he already possesses oceans of knowledge he cannot account for — logic, mathematics, and his own fork. He is like a thief caught with the loot who demands that the arresting officers produce the ownership papers for their squad car.

summary.heading: Objection: the fundamental laws are just a brute fact
summary.body:
Suppose the atheist concedes everything so far — Hume and quantum mechanics haven’t undermined the principle that everything has an explanation, science can’t explain its own fundamental laws, and philosophy is a real source of explanation. He might still say the fundamental laws simply *have* no explanation of any kind; everything else is explained by them, but they are just there. Feser notes that Mackie and Russell essentially held this.

Three problems:

1. It contradicts the **principle of sufficient reason**, which chapter 5 argued is true. So it is a nonstarter.
2. It is **ad hoc**: there is no motive for it except avoiding arguments like those in the book — ironic, since atheists often accuse theists of rigging premises to reach a desired conclusion. An independent motive would exist if the Humean or quantum-mechanical objections to PSR worked, but they don’t. And, as Lloyd Gerson observed (discussed in Part A), you cannot answer an argument that *offers* an explanation by saying “maybe there’s no explanation”; you must show what is wrong with the one given.
3. If the fundamental laws are unexplained, **no higher-level law explains anything** either. Explaining phenomenon P by law A, law A by law B, and then declaring B a brute fact is like setting a book on a shelf, the shelf on brackets, and then letting go of the brackets in midair and expecting everything to stay up. A regress of laws is like a hierarchical causal series (chapter 1): it must end in something self-explanatory that can impart explanatory power without borrowing it. Neither the unexplained nor the explained-by-another can do that; only what is purely actual, without parts, whose essence is existence, and so absolutely necessary.

summary.heading: Objection: a designer would be more complex than the universe
summary.body:
This objection, going back to Hume and pressed by Dawkins, says any designer of the universe would be even more complex than the universe and so would itself need a cause. Feser says it should be obvious by now what is wrong.

It targets **design arguments** of the Paley or Intelligent Design type: natural objects like the eye or bacterial flagellum have many parts arranged just so, like human artifacts, which have intelligent designers; so by analogy, probably the natural objects do too. The critic replies that a designer like us would be complex in the same way and need its own explanation, so a more parsimonious explanation is likely correct.

The five proofs are nothing like this:

- **No appeal to complexity** in that sense. The Neo-Platonic proof does start from things having parts, but it doesn’t care how many, whether they must be arranged precisely, or whether they resemble artifacts. A pebble or a drop of water — which Paley would never cite — works as well as an eye.
- **No appeal to probability.** The proofs concern hierarchical causal series operating here and now, not linear series stretching back to the origin of species. And they are attempted strict demonstrations, not inductive or abductive inferences, so it misses the point to propose that some rival explanation is more probable or parsimonious. To refute them you must show a premise is false, the conclusion doesn’t follow, or the argument begs the question.
- **Most importantly**, the proofs *agree* that a complex cause would need a cause. That is exactly why they conclude that the ultimate cause is absolutely simple, without parts. That is true of the God they reach and of no terminus the atheist proposes. As an objection to this kind of natural theology, it completely misses the point.

summary.heading: Objection: go “one god further”
summary.body:
Dawkins (in a lecture) and Colin McGinn (in print) argue that monotheists already reject Zeus, Venus, Thor, Quetzalcoatl and the rest, so to be consistent they should reject one more god. First reply: there are at least five demonstrations of the God of Western monotheism and no one claims arguments for Zeus. There is no inconsistency in affirming the one and denying the others, and anyone who says otherwise must answer the arguments rather than glibly lump God in with the pagan pantheon.

The deeper problem is that the objection misunderstands what the debate between atheism and classical theism (Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Maimonides, Avicenna, Aquinas, Leibniz) is about. It pictures God as one more member of a class of unusual “supernatural beings,” like werewolves or ghosts. But the God of classical theism is:

- not a member of any genus or species, including “gods,” since that would make him composite (genus plus difference), and he is simple;
- not sharing an essence with other “gods,” since that would mean a distinction of essence and existence in him, whereas he is existence itself;
- not one cause among many but the purely actual actualizer, the source of the causal power of everything else — including Zeus and company, were they real.

The pagan gods of the stories are limited: fluctuating emotions, bodies, beginnings, parents, frustrated plans, ignorance, vices. The God of classical theism is immutable, immaterial, eternal, uncaused, omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good. Each pagan god is *a being* among beings; God is not “a being” that has and derives existence but subsistent being itself, from which all else derives.

Feser’s analogies: imagine an anti-Euclidean who says, “You agree that every drawn triangle has imperfectly straight sides; I just go one step further and say triangularity itself has imperfectly straight sides.” Or an anti-Platonist: “You agree every good thing is imperfectly good; I just extend that to the Form of the Good.” These are category mistakes — treating the standard as one more instance measured by it. The point holds *whether or not* Euclid or Plato is right: if space is non-Euclidean, Euclidean triangles are simply uninstantiated, not imperfectly straight; if the Third Man argument works, there is no Form of the Good, not an imperfect one. Likewise, even if atheism were true, it would not be because God turned out to be one more nonexistent member of the class of gods. That suggestion does not even make sense.

summary.heading: Objection: the philosophers’ God is not the God of ordinary believers
summary.body:
Two problems. First, it would be **irrelevant** even if true: if the arguments work, the God of philosophical theism exists and atheism is false. The remaining debate — whether Judaism, Christianity, Islam, or some other religion adds revealed knowledge of this God — is an argument among theists.

Second, it is **false**. Some religions explicitly identify the two. Standard Catholic teaching holds that the God of the Bible is the same God knowable by philosophical argument: some truths about him (that he is omnipotent and omniscient) are knowable both by reason and by revelation, while others (that he is a Trinity) are knowable only by revelation — but it is one God known by different routes. Other religions make similar claims.

What about the ordinary person in the pew, who knows nothing of divine simplicity or act and potency? The ordinary person also has a crude picture of atoms and molecules — little balls joined by sticks — yet he really does believe in atoms; he just understands them less well than a physicist. Likewise the ordinary believer holds that God caused the world, is unique, uncaused, never came to be, all-powerful, all-knowing, all-good. He can’t articulate or defend these beliefs as a philosopher would, but it is the same God, less sophisticatedly understood.

summary.heading: The problem of evil (I): defense versus theodicy, and Mackie’s logical argument
summary.body:
Philosophers distinguish two questions: is evil logically consistent with God’s existence, and if so, why does God permit it? Answering the first is a **defense**; answering the second is a **theodicy**. (Feser notes older Thomistic works used “theodicy” as a synonym for natural theology in general.) One can show compatibility without claiming to know God’s specific reasons, and a defense suffices to rebut the objection, so that is Feser’s focus.

J. L. Mackie’s logical argument: God is supposedly omnipotent and wholly good; an omnipotent being faces no limits, and a good being eliminates evil as far as it can; so God would be able and willing to eliminate all evil; yet evil exists. Feser says chapter 6’s treatment of omnipotence and goodness shows the problem lies in the second premise, which fails twice:

- Omnipotence has limits of a kind: even God can’t make a round square or make 2 + 2 = 5, because contradictions aren’t things to be done. If some goods logically cannot be had without permitting certain evils, God can’t have the goods without the evils.
- A good being does *not* necessarily eliminate every evil it can, because doing so might eliminate goods that presuppose those evils. A good parent could remove the misery of homework by cancelling it, but won’t, since that would sacrifice the child’s learning and obedience.

The classic example is free will: it is good that there be free creatures rather than automata, but free creatures can do evil. Mackie replied that God could have made free creatures who always freely choose good. Some theists (Plantinga is the best known) deny that God could guarantee this. Feser says the theist need not take that route: grant Mackie that God could create a world with free will, no evil, and even morally significant choices (not murdering, not stealing). It still doesn’t follow that such a world could contain *all the moral goods of this one*. Forgiveness and mercy require real wrongdoing to forgive. Courage requires danger; compassion requires misfortune; sacrifice requires giving up something good. (He notes John Hick’s “soul-making” theme.) So it is not free will in the abstract that matters, but the virtues that only a world containing evil makes possible. Mackie’s argument fails — and Feser notes that Mackie himself later conceded that evil doesn’t show theism to be logically inconsistent.

A footnote adds that this is not Leibniz’s claim that this is the best possible world or that God must create the best: God could have created nothing, or a world better in various respects. The point is only that, having made this world, God permits its evils because he draws from them goods not otherwise possible.

summary.heading: The problem of evil (II): Rowe’s evidential argument and the afterlife
summary.body:
The later Mackie and others shifted to an **evidential argument**: evil doesn’t disprove God, but it makes his nonexistence probable. William Rowe’s influential version: a perfect being would prevent any suffering it could prevent without losing a greater good or permitting an equal or worse evil; probably some actual suffering is like that; so probably there is no such being. His example: a fawn trapped in a forest fire caused by lightning, burned, and suffering for days before dying — suffering that seems pointless, redeemed by no virtue-building. Rowe concedes we cannot prove or know with certainty that no greater good comes from it; he claims only that it is rational to believe none does.

Feser’s reply: that belief is rational only if we lack independent reason to think God exists — and thus independent reason to think there *must* be a greater good even where we can’t see it. We have such reasons: five demonstrations of God and further arguments that he is omnipotent, omniscient, and perfectly good. Since Rowe admits a hidden greater good is possible, he must admit that independent proof of God gives reason to think such a good is actual. So the evidential argument poses no challenge to the book’s arguments; to challenge them it would first have to refute them independently — and if it could, it wouldn’t be needed.

Feser adds that our ignorance of God’s reasons is exactly what we should expect, though fully showing this requires arguments beyond the book’s scope — especially for the immortality of the soul. Suppose there is an afterlife. Then this life’s evils could be unredeemable only if no good in the afterlife could outweigh them, which is absurd to claim: the afterlife would be endless while even the worst earthly sufferings end, and we are no more able to grasp it than a small child can grasp adulthood. Children often can’t see the point of homework, spinach, chores, or punishment until they grow up. God knows infinitely more than any parent, and the afterlife differs from this life far more than adulthood differs from childhood — so we should expect both that God can bring about an outweighing good and that we cannot yet see how. Developing this would be a theodicy; for a defense it is enough that such an afterlife is *possible*. Other aspects of evil (evil as privation; whether God must create the best world) were treated in chapter 6.

summary.heading: Objection: divine hiddenness
summary.body:
The hiddenness argument (associated with J. L. Schellenberg) rests on two assumptions: if God existed, his existence would be obvious to most people; and it is not. Feser questions both.

**First assumption.** Schellenberg grounds it in the claim that God would want an explicit, meaningful personal relationship with us, which presupposes our believing he exists. But not all theists think God intends that — Aristotle’s Unmoved Mover eternally contemplates itself and takes no notice of us — so as a general argument for atheism it is a nonstarter. Even for Jews and Christians, who (rightly, Feser says) believe God does seek relationship, the argument leaves untouched the attributes the proofs establish: one, simple, purely actual, immutable, immaterial, eternal, omnipotent, omniscient. If those are true, atheism is false. As for God’s goodness and love, the reply parallels the one to evil: given proof that a good and loving God exists, to whatever extent he hasn’t made himself more obvious there must be a greater good in it. Schellenberg would need to show no such good is possible, and there is no more reason to think that than to think no good could come from Rowe’s fawn — which even Rowe didn’t claim.

John Hick suggested God keeps an **epistemic distance** so we are free to choose a relationship with him. Feser thinks Hick greatly exaggerates this — the universe isn’t “religiously ambiguous,” since there are decisive arguments, and free choice about relating to God doesn’t depend on doubt, as the many believers throughout history who did terrible things without doubting God show. But there is a kernel of truth: God gives us a long leash in what we think as well as what we do. Philosophers have denied change, time, the material world, causation, free will, the self, even consciousness and thought. It’s unsurprising some deny God. Finite minds err; free wills can turn attention away from evidence; and people have motives for doing so. Such distance as exists follows from finitude and freedom.

**Second assumption.** Is God really not obvious to most people? Few know philosophical theism, but historically the vast majority of humans have been theists of some kind, and most still are — whether monotheist, pantheist, polytheist, or holding a vaguer sense of the divine — often with a confidence atheists complain about. If God is hidden from most people, most people haven’t noticed. The atheist may say their reasons are weak; but a layman’s weak grasp of the evidence for science doesn’t make scientific truths hidden from him, and the same goes for belief in a divine cause of the world, which often approximates the proofs in simplified form. Historically most experts — from Xenophanes, Plato, and Aristotle through Augustine, Anselm, Avicenna, Aquinas, Descartes, Leibniz, Newton, Locke, and many more — held that God’s existence can be known by argument, and many philosophers still do. To say those arguments have since been refuted begs the question. And if many intellectuals reject theism on the basis of incompetent objections like “what caused God?”, they have no standing to accuse ordinary believers of insufficient evidence. That they think God obviously hidden says more about their grasp of natural theology than about natural theology.

summary.heading: Objection: theistic arguments are just rationalizations
summary.body:
The claim that arguments for God merely dress up conclusions believers had already settled on is a textbook **ad hominem**, specifically **poisoning the well**: rejecting an argument because of the arguer’s supposed motives. Whether an argument is good is independent of the motives or character of whoever offers it.

The charge also cuts both ways. Someone can want God to exist and avoid looking hard at atheist arguments; someone else can want God *not* to exist and avoid looking hard at theist arguments. Feser cites Thomas Nagel’s candid admission that he hopes there is no God, doesn’t want the universe to be like that, and suspects this “cosmic authority problem” drives much of the scientism and reductionism of our time. None of this means all atheists — or all theists — are dishonest. The point is that motives are irrelevant: the only way to tell whether an argument is good is to examine it, not to hunt for excuses not to.

summary.heading: Objection: it can’t be a proof if so many people remain unconvinced
summary.body:
Three problems.

1. Many standard criticisms of these arguments are incompetent, aimed at caricatures and ignorant of what defenders actually said. Rejection by ill-informed critics is no evidence that a demonstration fails.
2. **Double standard.** Skeptics treat the mere existence of an objection to a theistic argument as showing the argument “fails,” as if a good argument must win universal assent. They never treat arguments for materialism or against free will that way — there, critics are just part of ongoing debate, and the argument stays on the table. Even eccentric philosophical positions get that courtesy; theistic arguments don’t, and Hume’s having said something two centuries ago is treated as a final refutation. Feser quotes Hilary Putnam in a footnote noting that by the “must convince every rational person” standard, the philosophical arguments of Frege, Russell, Quine, Davidson, and Lewis would all fail too.
3. Critics misunderstand what classical theists mean by **demonstration**: a conclusion that follows with deductive necessity from premises that are certain, their certainty established by metaphysical analysis. That makes it more secure than scientific inference in two respects: it is not probabilistic or an inference to the best explanation where an alternative might in principle be right; and its premises can’t be overturned by future empirical inquiry, because every possible inquiry presupposes them.

The Aristotelian proof illustrates: its first premise, that change occurs, is empirical in a sense (so the argument isn’t a priori), but no future experience could overturn it, because any future experience would itself be a change. We might empirically show a particular apparent change unreal, but not that all change is. The other premises (the principle of causality, the impossibility of an infinite hierarchical regress) are defended by metaphysical argument — e.g., causality follows from PSR, which can be defended by showing its denial is self-undermining. The other four proofs can be defended similarly.

Such arguments are ambitious, but nothing in their strategy implies every reader — even a fair-minded, informed one — will immediately see their force, or that no hard philosophical work is needed to defend the premises. Controversy does not entail failure. What a demonstration requires is that, when all is said and done, it can be defended against every objection claiming the conclusion doesn’t follow or a premise is doubtful. Feser claims the book has done that for all five proofs, and closes the book with the traditional sign-off of a completed proof: Q.E.D.
